Firing was more irregular in depleted mice, quantified as a significant increase in the coefficient of variation of the interspike interval (CVISI) (Figure 1E) (Median ±MAD: Ctl: 0.54 ± 0.13; Acute: 0.76 ± 0.24; Gradual: 0.68 ± 0.16; KW pairwise, Ctl vs. Acute, Grad, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Burst firing became more prevalent in dopamine depleted mice.
claims.source: Burst firing also became more prevalent in dopamine depleted mice, quantified using the Poisson Surprise method (Soares et al., 2004) (Figure 1F and see Materials and methods) (z-test, Ctl vs. Acute, Grad, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: No difference in fractional β power was observed between control, acutely depleted, and gradually depleted mice.
claims.source: We observed no difference in fractional β between Ctl, Acute and Grad mice (1-way ANOVA, p = 0.076), consistent with a previous report (Lobb et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: Elevated β-oscillations are not a robust feature of SNr pathophysiology in 6-OHDA depleted mice.
claims.source: These results suggest that elevated β-oscillations are not a robust feature of SNr pathophysiology in 6-OHDA depleted mice.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on β-oscillations.

claims.claim: The average percentage of synchronous pairs increased from 8.6 ± 7.8% in control mice to 30.6 ± 11.4% in acutely depleted mice and 28.0 ± 22.6% in gradually depleted mice.
claims.source: We found that the average percentage of synchronous pairs was 8.6 ± 7.8% (n = 7 animals) in control mice but increased to 30.6 ± 11.4% (n = 7 animals) and 28.0 ± 22.6% (n = 9 animals) in acutely and gradually depleted mice, respectively (Figure 1J) (Dunnett, Ctl vs. Acute, Grad, p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: A classifier was unable to discriminate acutely from gradually depleted mice above chance levels using pathophysiological metrics.
claims.source: The classifier was unable to discriminate these conditions above chance levels (Figure 1L) (60.2 ± 24% CI95, right-tail t-test vs. chance, 50%, p = 0.3842, n = 16 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from classification analysis shown in Figure 1L.

claims.claim: A classifier successfully discriminated end-stage mice (Grad +Acute) from control mice well above chance.
claims.source: By contrast, retraining the same model to discriminate end-stage mice (Grad +Acute) from control mice resulted in classification well above chance (Figure 1M) (84.9 ± 12% CI95, right-tail t-test vs. chance, 50%, p = 7.87×10−6, n = 23 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from classification analysis shown in Figure 1M.

claims.claim: Stereotyped changes in SNr physiology occur at end-stages of dopamine loss, regardless of whether dopamine is depleted slowly over a month, or acutely, over days.
claims.source: These results suggest that stereotyped changes in SNr physiology occur at end-stages of dopamine loss, regardless of whether dopamine is depleted slowly over a month, or acutely, over days.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification results comparing acute and gradual depletion models.

claims.claim: SNr firing rate was significantly reduced in the G85% group and remained suppressed as depletions progressed.
claims.source: The most sensitive parameter was firing rate (Figure 2C), which was significantly reduced in the earliest depletion group examined (G85%) and remained suppressed as depletions progressed (Median ±MAD: Ctl: 35 ± 11 Hz, n = 262 neurons/7 animals; G85%: 26 ± 12 Hz, n = 272/5; G60%: 27 ± 14 Hz, n = 318/7; G30%: 30 ± 10 Hz, n = 318/8; G5%: 26 ± 11 Hz, n = 293/9; KW pairwise, Ctl vs. 85%, 60%, 30%, 5%, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Firing irregularity (CVisi) in the G85% group was modestly, but significantly elevated relative to control but this difference became more pronounced at later depletion stages, with <60% dopamine remaining.
claims.source: Firing irregularity (CVisi) in the G85% group was modestly, but significantly elevated relative to control (Figure 2D) but this difference became more pronounced at later depletion stages, with <60% dopamine remaining (Figure 2D) (Median ±MAD: Ctl: 0.54 ± 0.13; G85%: 0.59 ± 0.15; G60%: 0.65 ± 0.20; G30%: 0.71 ± 0.22; G5%: 0.68 ± 0.16; KW pairwise, G85% vs. G30%, G5%, p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The proportion of 'highly bursty' neurons was relatively unchanged at early stages of depletion, but became pronounced with <60% dopamine remaining.
claims.source: Similarly, the proportion of 'highly bursty' neurons was relatively unchanged at early stages of depletion, but became pronounced with <60% dopamine remaining (Figure 2E) (z-test, Ctl vs. 60%, 30%, 5%, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The fraction of pairs firing synchronously did not reach statistical significance until end-stage depletion.
claims.source: The fraction of pairs firing synchronously in each animal tended to increase at intermediate stages of depletion, but did not reach statistical significance until end-stage (Figure 2F) (Ctl: 8.6 ± 7.8% n = 7 animals; G85%: 18 ± 14% n = 5 animals; G60%: 7.3 ± 7.3% n = 7 animals; G30%: 15 ± 11% n = 8 animals; G5%: 28 ± 23% n = 9 animals; Dunnett, Ctl vs. 5%, p = 0.04).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The physiological transition from control to fully depleted mice followed a biphasic decline.
claims.source: We observed that the physiological transition from control to fully depleted mice followed a biphasic decline (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the principal component analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: The first transition in SNr physiology occurred early in the depletion process, reflecting an acute sensitivity of SNr physiology to small changes in dopamine levels.
claims.source: The first transition occurred early in the depletion process, reflecting an acute sensitivity of SNr physiology to small changes in dopamine levels.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the biphasic decline observed in the principal component analysis.

claims.claim: After the initial drop in physiology PC1, it remained relatively stable across a wide range of dopamine levels but underwent a second sharp drop as mice reached the end-stage of depletion.
claims.source: After this initial drop, physiology PC1 remained relatively stable across a wide range of dopamine levels but underwent a second sharp drop as mice reached the end-stage of depletion.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the biphasic decline observed in the principal component analysis.

claims.claim: Early dopamine loss often resulted in modest hyperactivity relative to control mice, followed by hypoactivity at late depletion stages.
claims.source: Early dopamine loss often resulted in modest hyperactivity relative to control mice, followed by hypoactivity at late depletion stages, as observed in open field velocity (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from behavioral testing shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Velocity, rearing, and total time taken to complete the pole task were preserved until late stages of dopamine loss.
claims.source: Velocity, rearing, and total time taken to complete the pole task were preserved until late stages of dopamine loss (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from behavioral testing shown in Figures 3B-D.

claims.claim: Behavioral performance remained relatively intact until dopamine levels dropped below 25–35%, after which behavioral performance declined rapidly.
claims.source: Thus, behavioral performance remained relatively intact until dopamine levels dropped below 25–35%, after which behavioral performance declined rapidly (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral principal component analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The sharp transition in behavioral performance is similar to the pattern of symptomatic onset in human PD patients.
claims.source: This sharp transition is similar to the pattern of symptomatic onset in human PD patients (Bernheimer et al., 1973; Betarbet et al., 2002; Deumens et al., 2002; Fahn, 2003; Riederer and Wuketich, 1976).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to clinical literature supported by citations.

claims.claim: Changes in physiology and behavior are correlated over the course of dopamine loss.
claims.source: Optimal behavioral prediction depended on physiology (y, y3), dopamine (x, x2), and their interaction (y*x2) (95% confidence interval on coefficients, Adj-R2 = 0.615, Figure 3H), suggesting physiology and behavior are correlated over the course of dopamine loss.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the 2D polynomial fit shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Early changes in physiology align with the prodromal period, while late changes in physiology align with the symptomatic period.
claims.source: This overlay reveals that early changes in physiology align with the prodromal period, while late changes in physiology align with the symptomatic period.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between physiology, behavior, and dopamine levels shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Striatal inoculation with preformed fibrils of α-syn (PFF α-syn) resulted in progressive dopamine loss and the formation of Lewy body-like inclusions.
claims.source: Striatal inoculation with preformed fibrils of α-syn (PFF α-syn) resulted in progressive dopamine loss and the formation of Lewy body-like inclusions (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the PFF α-syn model shown in Figures 4A-B.

claims.claim: Even after 6 months, striatal TH levels in PFF α-syn mice did not drop below 30%.
claims.source: Even after 6 months, striatal TH levels did not drop below 30%, thus end-stage physiological deficits could not be examined in the PFF α-syn model.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the PFF α-syn model.

claims.claim: PFF α-Syn mice showed trends towards modest hyperactivity, similar to gradually depleted mice.
claims.source: Mice with 85–30% dopamine remaining showed trends towards modest hyperactivity, similar to gradually depleted mice (Figure 4C–F), however the only group with significant differences from control was an increase in open field velocity in Syn60% mice.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from behavioral testing in PFF α-syn mice shown in Figures 4C-F.

claims.claim: Behavioral scores of PFF α-Syn mice were similar to that of 6-OHDA-treated mice at similar stages of depletion.
claims.source: Although PFF α-Syn mice did not reach end-stage depletion levels and therefore did not transition into the symptomatic stage, their behavioral scores were similar to that of 6-OHDA-treated mice at similar stages of depletion.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of behavioral data between PFF α-syn and 6-OHDA models.

claims.claim: SNr firing rates in PFF α-syn mice were significantly reduced even at the earliest stage of depletion, and this decrease persisted across subsequent stages of depletion.
claims.source: SNr firing rates were significantly reduced even at the earliest stage of depletion, and this decrease persisted across subsequent stages of depletion (Figure 5A) (Median ±MAD: Control: 35 ± 11 Hz, n = 262 neurons/7 animals; Syn85%: 26 ± 11 Hz, n = 98/3; Syn60%: 25 ± 9 Hz, n = 155/4; Syn30%: 25 ± 8 Hz, n = 150/3; KW pairwise, Ctl vs. 85%, 60%, 30%, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from PFF α-syn mice supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Changes in firing patterns in PFF α-syn mice emerged at later stages of depletion (<60% remaining), mirroring the progression observed in 6-OHDA-treated mice.
claims.source: Changes in firing patterns emerged at later stages of depletion (<60% remaining), mirroring the progression observed in 6-OHDA-treated mice.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of physiological data between PFF α-syn and 6-OHDA models.

claims.claim: The progression of SNr pathophysiology depends more on the magnitude of dopamine depletion than the depletion model.
claims.source: Combined with results from 6-OHDA-treated mice, our data suggest that the progression of SNr pathophysiology depends more on the magnitude of dopamine depletion than the depletion model.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between 6-OHDA and PFF α-syn models.

claims.claim: A significant increase in TH immunoreactivity was observed on the contralateral side in unilaterally depleted mice, suggestive of compensatory mechanisms engaged within the dopamine system.
claims.source: A significant increase in TH immunoreactivity was observed on the contralateral side (211 ± 91%) (Figure 6B), suggestive of compensatory mechanisms engaged within the dopamine system (Zigmond et al., 1990; Zigmond et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from unilateral depletion experiments with interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Firing rates of SNr neurons in the depleted hemisphere of unilaterally depleted mice were reduced relative to control, and the magnitude of this change was similar to that seen in bilaterally depleted mice.
claims.source: Firing rates of SNr neurons in the depleted hemisphere were reduced relative to control (Median ±MAD: Ctl: 35 ± 11 Hz, n = 262 neurons/7 animals; Ipsiuni: 26 ± 9 Hz, n = 136 neurons/6 animals; KW pairwise, Ctl vs. Ipsiuni, p < 0.0001), and the magnitude of this change was similar to that seen in bilaterally depleted mice (Figure 6C) (KW pairwise, Ipsiuni vs. G5%, p = 0.842).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from unilateral depletion experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Firing rates in the contralateral SNr of unilaterally depleted mice were similar to those observed in control mice.
claims.source: Firing rates in the contralateral SNr were similar to those observed in control mice (Figure 6C) (Median ±MAD: Ctl: 35 ± 11 Hz, n = 262 neurons/7animals; Contrauni: 37 ± 14 Hz, n = 94 neurons/5 animals) (KW pairwise, Ctl vs. Contrauni, p = 0.712).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from unilateral depletion experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Firing irregularity (CVisi) was significantly elevated in both hemispheres of unilaterally depleted mice, and this effect was stronger in the ipsilateral hemisphere compared to the contralateral hemisphere.
claims.source: Firing irregularity (CVisi) was significantly elevated on both sides, and this effect was stronger in the ipsilateral hemisphere compared to the contralateral hemisphere (Figure 6D) (Median ±MAD: Ctl: 0.54 ± 0.13 n = 262 neurons/7 animals; Ipsiuni: 0.86 ± 0.30, n = 136 neurons/6 animals; Contrauni: 0.72 ± 0.22, n = 94 neurons/5 animals; KW pairwise, Ctl vs. Ipsiuni, Contrauni, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from unilateral depletion experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: A classifier was unable to discriminate end-stage physiology above chance levels among four end-stage categories (A5%, G5%, Ipsiuni and Ipsiasym conditions).
claims.source: The classifier was unable to discriminate end-stage physiology above chance levels (30.4 ± 6.3% accuracy, right-tail t-test vs. chance = 25%; p = 0.1986; n = 33 mice) (Figure 6N).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from classification analysis shown in Figure 6N.

claims.claim: Combined Ipsiuni and Ipsiasym hemispheres were discriminated from Ctl mice with 84.7 ± 5.9% accuracy.
claims.source: By contrast, combined Ipsiuni and Ipsiasym hemispheres were discriminated from Ctl mice with 84.7 ± 5.9% accuracy (Figure 6O) (right-tail t-test vs. chance, 50%; p = 3.59 × 10−6, n = 23 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from classification analysis shown in Figure 6O.

claims.claim: End-stage SNr physiology shows stereotyped pathophysiology across different depletion models.
claims.source: Thus, end-stage SNr physiology shows stereotyped pathophysiology across different depletion models.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification results across multiple depletion models.

claims.claim: A multinomial classifier successfully separated mice into 'early', 'intermediate', and 'late' depletion groups 52.9% of the time, significantly more often than expected by chance (33%).
claims.source: The multinomial classifier successfully separated mice into each of these groups 52.9% of the time, significantly more often than expected by chance (33%) (Figure 7C) (multi-class Matthew's Correlation Coefficient = 0.25, p = 0.004, permutation test).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from classification analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Over the course of dopamine loss, deterioration of SNr physiology occurs as a series of state transitions: from 'normal' to 'moderate', and from 'moderate' to 'severe'.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that over the course of dopamine loss, deterioration of SNr physiology occurs as a series of state transitions: from 'normal' to 'moderate', and from 'moderate' to 'severe'.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification results and physiological progression data.

claims.claim: Transitions from the normal to moderate state were driven by increased irregularity, and firing rate interactions with spike patterns.
claims.source: These results suggest that transitions from the normal to moderate state were driven by increased irregularity, and firing rate interactions with spike patterns (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the multinomial classifier coefficients shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Transitions from the moderate to severe state were driven by increased synchrony.
claims.source: Transitions from the moderate to severe state were driven by increased synchrony (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the multinomial classifier coefficients shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: During early dopamine loss, decreases in firing rate and increases in synchrony pushed the SNr towards pathology, transitioning from a 'normal' to 'moderate' pathophysiological state.
claims.source: During early dopamine loss, decreases in firing rate and increases in synchrony pushed the SNr towards pathology, transitioning from a 'normal' to 'moderate' pathophysiological state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the similarity to end-stage analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: As dopamine loss progressed, increases in irregularity and bursting promoted further dysfunction, but were offset by a decrease in synchrony and partial recovery of firing rate, keeping the SNr buffered in a 'moderate' pathophysiological state.
claims.source: As dopamine loss progressed, increases in irregularity and bursting promoted further dysfunction, but were offset by a decrease in synchrony and partial recovery of firing rate. These changes opposed dysfunction and possibly kept the SNr buffered in a 'moderate' pathophysiological state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the similarity to end-stage analysis shown in Figure 7E with speculation about buffering mechanisms.

claims.claim: At late stages of dopamine loss, buffering broke down and dysfunction aligned across all physiological parameters, transitioning the SNr into a final, 'severe' pathophysiological state.
claims.source: At late stages of dopamine loss, however, this buffering broke down and dysfunction aligned across all physiological parameters, transitioning the SNr into a final, 'severe' pathophysiological state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the similarity to end-stage analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: SNr pathophysiology progresses in discrete stages, rather than smoothly as a function of dopamine loss.
claims.source: The finding that SNr pathophysiology progresses in discrete stages, rather than smoothly as a function of dopamine loss, suggests different windows of opportunity for delivering specific therapies.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings with implications for therapy.

claims.claim: Interventions that preferentially affect firing rate (i.e. L-DOPA) are predicted to be more effective at earlier stages of depletion rather than late.
claims.source: Our results predict that interventions that preferentially affect firing rate (i.e. L-DOPA) are more likely to be effective at earlier stages of depletion rather than late, whereas interventions that preferentially affect regularity and synchrony (i.e. DBS) are more likely to be effective at late stages of depletion (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings about the timing of different physiological changes.

claims.claim: Interventions that preferentially affect regularity and synchrony (i.e. DBS) are predicted to be more effective at late stages of depletion.
claims.source: Our results predict that interventions that preferentially affect firing rate (i.e. L-DOPA) are more likely to be effective at earlier stages of depletion rather than late, whereas interventions that preferentially affect regularity and synchrony (i.e. DBS) are more likely to be effective at late stages of depletion (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings about the timing of different physiological changes.

claims.claim: Motor symptoms emerge when the SNr is in the severe pathological state, which requires alignment of pathophysiology across many different parameters.
claims.source: Our model reconciles this apparent paradox by predicting that motor symptoms emerge when the SNr is in the severe pathological state, which requires alignment of pathophysiology across many different parameters.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Changes in any individual parameter would be sufficient to transition the SNr out of the severe pathological state and into the moderate pathophysiological state, where few if any motor deficits are observed.
claims.source: Conversely, our data predict that changes in any individual parameter would be sufficient to transition the SNr out of the severe pathological state and into the moderate pathophysiological state, where few if any motor deficits are observed.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings about physiological states.

claims.claim: Levodopa (L-DOPA) restores movement predominantly through effects on firing rates.
claims.source: This prediction is supported by findings that Levodopa (L-DOPA) restores movement predominantly through effects on firing rates (Aristieta et al., 2016; Hernandez et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2018; Ryan et al., 2018) whereas DBS restores movement predominantly through effects on firing patterns (Birdno and Grill, 2008; McCairn and Turner, 2009; McCairn et al., 2015; Zhuang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: DBS restores movement predominantly through effects on firing patterns.
claims.source: This prediction is supported by findings that Levodopa (L-DOPA) restores movement predominantly through effects on firing rates (Aristieta et al., 2016; Hernandez et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2018; Ryan et al., 2018) whereas DBS restores movement predominantly through effects on firing patterns (Birdno and Grill, 2008; McCairn and Turner, 2009; McCairn et al., 2015; Zhuang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Amplified β-oscillations were not detectable in mouse SNr.
claims.source: Most physiological changes observed in the SNr were consistent with previous literature, with two exceptions: amplified β-oscillations were not detectable in mouse SNr (see also Lobb et al., 2013), and SNr firing rates in our study were decreased by depletion, rather than increased, as predicted by the classical 'rate model' (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: SNr firing rates in this study were decreased by depletion, rather than increased, as predicted by the classical 'rate model'.
claims.source: Most physiological changes observed in the SNr were consistent with previous literature, with two exceptions: amplified β-oscillations were not detectable in mouse SNr (see also Lobb et al., 2013), and SNr firing rates in our study were decreased by depletion, rather than increased, as predicted by the classical 'rate model' (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation that differs from the classical rate model.

claims.claim: Experimental measures of firing rate changes in the SNr following dopamine depletion have varied widely in their magnitude and direction across studies.
claims.source: However, experimental measures of firing rate changes in the SNr following dopamine depletion have varied widely in their magnitude and direction across studies (Seeger-Armbruster and von Ameln-Mayerhofer, 2013a).
claims.evidence: This statement summarizes findings from the literature supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A decrease in current from type three canonical transient receptor potential channels (TRPC3) that is important for intrinsic pacemaking in the SNr might account for the firing rate decreases observed in this study.
claims.source: One mechanism that might account for the firing rate decreases observed in our study is a decrease in current from type three canonical transient receptor potential channels (TRPC3) that is important for intrinsic pacemaking in the SNr (Zhou, 2010; Zhou and Lee, 2011; Zhou et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation supported by citations.

claims.claim: TRPC3 channels are positively modulated by D1/5 receptors and their blockade has been shown to slow firing rates and promote irregular firing patterns.
claims.source: TRPC3 channels are positively modulated by D1/5 receptors and their blockade has been shown to slow firing rates and promote irregular firing patterns.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about TRPC3 channels.

claims.claim: Firing rate changes that take place in the SNr might be different than those in the internal globus pallidus (GPi).
claims.source: Firing rate changes that take place in the SNr might also be different than those in the internal globus pallidus (GPi), the basal ganglia output nucleus that is preferentially targeted in human and primate studies.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about differences between brain regions.

claims.claim: In a primate MPTP model, firing rate changes were more prominent in the GPi than in the SNr.
claims.source: In a primate MPTP model, firing rate changes were more prominent in the GPi than in the SNr (Wichmann et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Most neurons in rodent SNr encode motor information and can influence movement either through projections to motor thalamus or through projections to locomotor brainstem.
claims.source: By comparison, most neurons in rodent SNr encode motor information (Barter et al., 2015; Rossi et al., 2016) and can influence movement either through projections to motor thalamus or through projections to locomotor brainstem (Capelli et al., 2017; Roseberry et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Compensatory plasticity is thought to play a major role in delaying the onset of motor symptoms until late stages of dopamine loss.
claims.source: Compensatory plasticity is thought to play a major role in delaying the onset of motor symptoms until late stages of dopamine loss.
claims.evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Evidence of compensatory plasticity is seen throughout the basal ganglia and dopamine system including increased sensitivity to dopamine, synaptic and intrinsic changes within the striatum, and plasticity in the GPe/STN.
claims.source: Evidence of compensatory plasticity is seen throughout the basal ganglia and dopamine system including increased sensitivity to dopamine (Bezard and Gross, 1998; Roedter et al., 2001; Schwarting and Huston, 1996; Zigmond et al., 1990; Zigmond et al., 2002), synaptic and intrinsic changes within the striatum (Blesa et al., 2012; Day et al., 2006; Escande et al., 2016; Fieblinger et al., 2014; Fuller et al., 2014; Gittis et al., 2011; Taverna et al., 2008), and plasticity in the GPe/STN (Chu et al., 2015; Chu et al., 2017; Fan et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The results suggest a role for compensatory plasticity in maintaining the intermediate physiological state in the SNr.
claims.source: Our results suggest a role for compensatory plasticity in maintaining the intermediate physiological state in the SNr.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: At early stages of dopamine loss, SNr firing rates were initially decreased, but moved towards higher values as burst firing and irregularity became more severe.
claims.source: At early stages of dopamine loss, SNr firing rates were initially decreased, but moved towards higher values as burst firing and irregularity became more severe (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the similarity to end-stage analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Bursting/irregularity may emerge as a result of compensatory mechanisms engaged to counteract aberrant firing rates.
claims.source: Although we do not know the cellular mechanisms driving these physiological changes, they are consistent with hypotheses that bursting/irregularity emerge as a result of compensatory mechanisms engaged to counteract aberrant firing rates.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: In the striatum, firing rate changes in spiny projection neurons (SPNs) drive plasticity of inhibitory microcircuits that promote synchrony.
claims.source: In the striatum, firing rate changes in spiny projection neurons (SPNs) drive plasticity of inhibitory microcircuits that promote synchrony (Gittis et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Synchronized output of the striatum can promote irregular, burst/pause firing in the GPe, which further amplifies pathological synchrony throughout the circuit.
claims.source: Synchronized output of the striatum can in turn promote irregular, burst/pause firing in the GPe (Kita and Kita, 2011), which further amplifies pathological synchrony throughout the circuit (Corbit et al., 2016; Sharott et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Firing rate changes have been shown to drive plasticity of connections between the GPe and STN, promoting oscillatory entrainment between these structures and contributing to pathological synchrony observed at later stages of depletion.
claims.source: Firing rate changes have also been shown to drive plasticity of connections between the GPe and STN, promoting oscillatory entrainment between these structures and contributing to pathological synchrony observed at later stages of depletion (Chu et al., 2015; Chu et al., 2017; Fan et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The severe physiological state at end-stage was stereotyped across models, regardless of the time course or symmetry of depletions.
claims.source: This severe physiological state was stereotyped across models, regardless of the time course or symmetry of depletions, suggesting that end-stage physiological deficits are not influenced by previous compensation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings across multiple depletion models.

claims.claim: The transition from the asymptomatic to the symptomatic stage represents the tipping point at which the compensatory capabilities of the system become overwhelmed by the severity of dopamine depletion.
claims.source: These results suggest that the transition from the asymptomatic to the symptomatic stage represents the tipping point at which the compensatory capabilities of the system become overwhelmed by the severity of dopamine depletion.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with speculation about compensatory mechanisms.

claims.claim: Recordings targeted to the SNr were confirmed by the presence of fast, tonically active units (~30–40% were modulated by movement), and by visualizing the recording track postmortem with immunostaining against the microglial marker, Iba-1.
claims.source: Recordings targeted to the SNr were confirmed by the presence of fast, tonically active units (~30–40% were modulated by movement), and by visualizing the recording track postmortem with immunostaining against the microglial marker, Iba-1 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the methods used to confirm recording locations.

claims.claim: Striatal TH levels were 4.1 ± 2.6% (relative to control) in acutely depleted mice and 3.7 ± 4.4% in gradually depleted mice.
claims.source: On average, striatal TH levels were 4.1 ± 2.6% (relative to control) in acutely depleted mice and 3.7 ± 4.4% in gradually depleted mice.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments.

claims.claim: Mice at advanced stages of depletion rarely initiated movements on the wheel (<2% of time spent moving).
claims.source: Because mice at advanced stages of depletion rarely initiated movements on the wheel (<2% of time spent moving), SNr physiology across conditions was compared during periods of rest (see: Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about mouse behavior.

claims.claim: The model fit to gradually depleted mouse physiology PC1 scores overlapped almost identically with the mean physiology PC1 score calculated from acutely depleted mice.

results.result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about Parkinson's disease, including its motor symptoms, the role of dopamine depletion in basal ganglia dysfunction, and existing theoretical models (rate model and pattern model) that attempt to explain motor deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C11 are well-supported by established knowledge and citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of PD pathophysiology and provide appropriate context for the study.

results.result: The manuscript identifies a gap in the field: while individual physiological parameters of basal ganglia dysfunction are well-established, their correlations with motor symptoms are weak, and most studies examine only end-stage depletion. Early intervention during the prodromal phase could improve patient outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C12-C13 are supported by citations to clinical and experimental literature. These claims accurately identify limitations in prior work and establish the rationale for studying progressive dopamine depletion.

results.result: At end-stage dopamine depletion (acute and gradual models with ~4% striatal TH remaining), SNr neurons show decreased firing rates, increased irregularity (CVISI), increased burst firing, and increased synchronous pairs compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19, C22, and C86 present primary experimental findings with appropriate statistical tests (Kruskal-Wallis, z-tests, Dunnett post-hoc) and adequate sample sizes. The data are shown in Figure 1D-F, J with clear quantification and significance levels reported.

results.result: Beta oscillations (13-30 Hz) were not significantly elevated in 6-OHDA depleted mice compared to controls, suggesting that elevated β-oscillations are not a robust feature of SNr pathophysiology in this mouse model.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 and C67 are supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA, p=0.076) and are consistent with a previous report (Lobb et al., 2013). The negative result is appropriately reported and interpreted.

results.result: A machine learning classifier could not discriminate between acute and gradual depletion models at end-stage (60.2% accuracy, not above chance), but successfully discriminated end-stage mice from controls (84.9% accuracy), indicating stereotyped SNr pathophysiology at end-stage regardless of depletion rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by appropriate classification analysis with cross-validation (jackknife procedure) and statistical testing (right-tail t-tests). The methodology is described in detail in Materials and Methods, and results are shown in Figure 1L-M.

results.result: During gradual dopamine depletion, firing rate decreases occur early (at 85% TH remaining) and persist, while changes in irregularity and bursting emerge more gradually and become pronounced at <60% TH remaining. Synchrony increases significantly only at end-stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are supported by statistical analysis across multiple depletion stages with appropriate post-hoc tests. The hierarchical progression of physiological changes is clearly demonstrated in Figure 2C-F with adequate sample sizes at each stage.

results.result: Principal component analysis reveals that SNr physiology follows a biphasic decline during gradual dopamine depletion: an initial early transition reflecting acute sensitivity to dopamine loss, followed by a stable intermediate period, and a final sharp decline at end-stage. The gradual depletion model accurately predicts acute depletion physiology at end-stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 and C88 are supported by PCA analysis (Figure 2H-I) with appropriate polynomial fitting (Adj-R²=0.368). The biphasic pattern is clearly visible and the overlap between gradual and acute models at end-stage validates the interpretation.

results.result: Behavioral deficits (open field velocity, rearing, pole task, wire hang) remain relatively intact until dopamine levels drop below 25-35%, after which performance declines rapidly. This sharp transition mirrors symptomatic onset in human PD patients. The gradual depletion model accurately predicts acute depletion behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 and C89 are supported by behavioral testing across multiple tasks with PCA analysis (Figure 3A-G). The polynomial fit (Adj-R²=0.545) demonstrates the monophasic behavioral decline, and comparison to clinical literature is appropriately cited.

results.result: A 2D polynomial model shows that physiology and behavior are correlated over the course of dopamine loss (Adj-R²=0.615), with early physiological changes aligning with the prodromal period and late changes aligning with the symptomatic period.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are supported by 2D polynomial regression analysis (Figure 3H) with appropriate model selection based on confidence intervals of coefficients. The relationship between physiology, behavior, and dopamine levels is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Striatal inoculation with preformed α-synuclein fibrils (PFF α-syn) produces progressive dopamine loss and Lewy body-like inclusions over 2-6 months, but TH levels do not drop below 30% even after 6 months, preventing examination of end-stage pathophysiology in this model.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 and C90-C91 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 4A-B) and citations to prior literature establishing the PFF α-syn model. The limitation of not reaching end-stage is clearly acknowledged.

results.result: PFF α-syn mice at intermediate depletion stages (85-30% TH remaining) show behavioral trends similar to 6-OHDA gradual depletion mice, including modest hyperactivity, though most differences from control are not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by behavioral testing (Figure 4C-H) with appropriate statistical analysis. The similarity to 6-OHDA mice is demonstrated through PCA and polynomial fitting, though the lack of statistical significance for most measures is appropriately noted.

results.result: In PFF α-syn mice, SNr firing rates decrease early (at 85% TH) and persist, while changes in firing patterns (irregularity, bursting) emerge at later stages (<60% TH), mirroring the progression in 6-OHDA mice. This suggests SNr pathophysiology depends more on dopamine depletion magnitude than depletion model.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 5A-C) with appropriate statistical analysis. The comparison between PFF α-syn and 6-OHDA models is valid and supports the interpretation that pathophysiology is stereotyped across models.

results.result: In unilaterally depleted mice, the ipsilateral (depleted) hemisphere shows reduced firing rates and elevated irregularity similar to bilateral depletion, while the contralateral hemisphere shows normal firing rates but elevated irregularity. Increased TH immunoreactivity in the contralateral hemisphere (211±91%) suggests compensatory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by electrophysiology and immunohistochemistry data (Figure 6A-E) with appropriate statistical analysis. The interpretation of compensatory mechanisms is supported by citations to prior literature on dopamine system compensation.

results.result: A classifier cannot discriminate among four end-stage depletion models (acute, gradual, unilateral ipsilateral, asymmetric ipsilateral) above chance (30.4% vs 25% chance), but successfully discriminates combined end-stage conditions from controls (84.7% accuracy), demonstrating stereotyped end-stage pathophysiology across models.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by multinomial classification analysis (Figure 6N-O) with appropriate cross-validation and statistical testing. The inability to discriminate among end-stage models supports the conclusion of stereotyped pathophysiology.

results.result: A multinomial classifier successfully separates mice into 'early', 'intermediate', and 'late' depletion groups 52.9% of the time (significantly above 33% chance, p=0.004), suggesting SNr physiology deteriorates through discrete state transitions: normal → moderate → severe.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by multinomial classification analysis (Figure 7C) with appropriate statistical testing (multi-class Matthew's Correlation Coefficient, permutation test). The three-state model is validated by the classifier's performance.

results.result: Analysis of multinomial classifier coefficients reveals that transitions from normal to moderate state are driven by increased irregularity and firing rate interactions with spike patterns, while transitions from moderate to severe state are driven by increased synchrony.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by examination of model coefficients (Figure 7D) with significance determined by 95% confidence intervals. The interpretation is consistent with the hierarchical progression of physiological changes observed in earlier results.

results.result: Cross-correlation analysis of physiological parameters with end-stage values reveals that during early depletion, firing rate decreases and synchrony increases push SNr toward pathology (normal→moderate transition). During intermediate stages, increases in irregularity and bursting are offset by decreased synchrony and partial firing rate recovery, buffering the SNr in a moderate state. At late stages, buffering breaks down and all parameters align, transitioning to severe pathophysiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 and C78 are supported by similarity-to-end-stage analysis (Figure 7E) using cross-correlation with smoothing spline fits. The interpretation of buffering and breakdown is consistent with the observed biphasic physiological progression and provides a mechanistic framework.

results.result: The study's main finding is that SNr pathophysiology progresses through discrete state transitions (normal→moderate→severe) that are highly stereotyped across depletion models and correlate with prodromal and symptomatic behavioral stages. The SNr is initially sensitive to small dopamine decreases, remains buffered in a moderate state across a range of dopamine levels, then transitions to severe pathophysiology when dopamine drops below 25-35%.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C14-C16 represent the study's central conclusions and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data across multiple depletion models, classification analyses, and correlation with behavior. The discrete state model is validated by multiple independent analyses.

results.result: The discrete progression of SNr pathophysiology suggests different therapeutic windows: interventions affecting firing rate (e.g., L-DOPA) are predicted to be more effective at early stages, while interventions affecting regularity and synchrony (e.g., DBS) are predicted to be more effective at late stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are predictions based on the experimental findings but lack direct experimental validation. While the predictions are logical extensions of the data and consistent with cited literature on L-DOPA and DBS mechanisms (C65-C66), they remain speculative without testing in the current study.

results.result: The study proposes a mechanistic model to explain the paradox that individual physiological parameters correlate with symptom alleviation but rarely predict symptom onset: motor symptoms emerge when the SNr is in the severe state (requiring alignment of multiple parameters), while changes in any single parameter can transition the SNr out of the severe state to the moderate state where motor deficits are minimal.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 provide a mechanistic interpretation supported by the experimental data showing hierarchical progression of physiological changes and their correlation with behavior. The model reconciles prior contradictory findings cited in the literature (C98-C99), though direct experimental validation of the prediction in C64 is not provided.

results.result: The study found decreased SNr firing rates with dopamine depletion, contrary to the classical rate model's prediction of increased rates. This discrepancy is discussed in the context of variable findings across studies, potential mechanisms involving TRPC3 channels, and possible differences between rodent SNr and primate GPi.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 appropriately discuss the unexpected finding of decreased firing rates. The discussion acknowledges variability in the literature (C69), proposes a plausible mechanism (C70-C71), and considers species/regional differences (C72-C74), all supported by appropriate citations. The speculation is clearly identified as such.

results.result: The study discusses the role of compensatory plasticity in maintaining the intermediate physiological state. Evidence from the literature shows compensation throughout the basal ganglia system, and the current results suggest bursting/irregularity may emerge as compensatory mechanisms to counteract aberrant firing rates, with circuit-level plasticity promoting pathological synchrony at later stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 and C79-C82 provide a speculative mechanistic interpretation of the intermediate buffered state. While the interpretation is consistent with cited literature on compensatory plasticity and the observed physiological progression, the study does not directly test compensatory mechanisms or establish causal relationships between firing rate changes and subsequent pattern changes.

results.result: The stereotyped severe physiological state at end-stage across all depletion models (regardless of time course or symmetry) suggests that end-stage deficits are not influenced by previous compensation, and the transition to the symptomatic stage represents the tipping point where compensatory capabilities are overwhelmed.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 are supported by the classification analyses showing inability to discriminate among end-stage models (C50, C52) and the convergence of all models to similar end-stage physiology. The interpretation about compensation being overwhelmed is reasonable given the data, though speculative elements are appropriately identified.

results.result: The study employed appropriate methodological controls: SNr recording locations were confirmed by physiological criteria and post-mortem immunohistochemistry, rest periods were used for analysis due to minimal movement in depleted mice, and TH immunoreactivity was validated as a measure of dopamine levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C87, and C93 describe methodological validations that are appropriately documented. The recording location confirmation (C85) is shown in Figure 1B, the rest period analysis rationale (C87) is clearly stated, and TH immunoreactivity validation (C93) is supported by citation.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within prior literature on therapeutic mechanisms (L-DOPA affects firing rates, DBS affects patterns), clinical observations (β-oscillations in humans, asymmetric dopamine loss), and the paradox that individual parameters correlate with symptom alleviation but not onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 and C92-C102 accurately represent prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings and are used to support the study's mechanistic model.
